💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I've recently introduced a few friends to the power of a great robot vacuum.
  • Recent findings suggest that the best robot vacuums these days aren’t just vacuuming your floors, nor are they blindly bumping around your house like they used to.
  • Sources indicate that here are the best robot vacuum cleaners I’ve tried this year, and everything we really liked from recent years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I've recently introduced a few friends to the power of a great robot vacuum. One of my friends calls hers a marriage saver, while the other was both thrilled and horrified by how many stains the vacuum’s AI found on her floors. Personally, my robot vacuums keep me from wanting to set the litter box on fire, since my cat is on a mission to create his own navigational trail of litter through my home.

Recent findings suggest that the best robot vacuums these days aren’t just vacuuming your floors, nor are they blindly bumping around your house like they used to. These gadgets are mopping, scrubbing away stains, lifting themselves off obstacles, and even reminding you to clean the dirtier areas in your home more frequently. A good robot vacuum can cost a pretty penny, but it doesn’t have to, depending on what you’re looking for. Which is the best model for you? I’ve been testing every latest robot vacuum I can in my three-story home filled with three adults, a preschooler, and a cat.

Sources indicate that here are the best robot vacuum cleaners I’ve tried this year, and everything we really liked from recent years. Looking for more vacuum ideas? Don't miss our guides to the Best Dyson Vacuums, Best Cordless Vacuums, Best Vacuums for Pet Hair, Best Carpet Cleaners, and Best Vacuums.

Industry observers note that updated November 2026: The Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro is now this guide's budget pick, with the Eufy Omni C28 as a budget runner-up. I've also added the Roborock Saros 20 Flow to Honorable Mentions, and testing notes on the Dyson Nurovi R3, Tapo RV50 Pro Omni, and three iRobot Roomba models (Max 875, Plus 678, and Plus 575). I've also ensured up-to-date links and prices.

Industry observers note that I’ve been testing the latest models from our favorite cleaning brands. Here are the top three I’d buy right now.

I was surprised how much I liked the AI-powered Shark PowerDetect UV Reveal. Its UV light revealed spots on my floor where I know I previously had spills, and its built-in AI had the vacuum go back over to deep-clean those spots in a way I clearly hadn’t done before. The UV Reveal also did a great job on my hard floors (both LVP and tile) as a mop-and-vacuum combo, as well as on my builder-grade carpet and a large rug in the living room. I was impressed that the rug actually felt just as fluffy and well-vacuumed as if I had cracked out my favorite Dyson stick vacuum instead of just sending a robot vacuum to do the work for me.

It has been revealed that it has an extendable arm, which did a good job passing my corner test. I stuck three Cheerios in tricky corners of my home, and it got two out of three, doing better than the latest Dyson vacuum. It managed to get the trickier two corners too; it skipped the third Cheerio to avoid bumping my bar stools. I also did a spill test with two spots of cherry juice in my home. It mopped away the first spill with no problem, but I did have to send it back out to finish cleaning the second spill. The UV Reveal did great with obstacle avoidance and has “NeverStuck Technology” to lift itself off obstacles, and it worked to get itself off the flat, long legs of one of my side tables. The vacuum finished a cleaning run in a good amount of time, cleaning my entire main floor in about 60 minutes, but it does go back out to scrub all the spots it sees on the floor. That took another 30 minutes for me, but I assume that would get shorter over time, the longer you live with this vacuum and have it cleaning up. Still, 93 minutes to run through four rooms and go back to do some scrub work is a solid time window.

Recent findings suggest that overall, this vacuum really shines on hard floors, but I also liked it on rugs and carpet if you have a mix of these in your home. It has an auto-empty base with a bagless debris system, so you won’t need to worry about purchasing debris bags to empty the docking station. The only downside is that the vacuum can learn only a single map, so it doesn’t work for multiple floors of your home unless you’re game for it to remap every time (which takes only a couple minutes, so it’s not a horrible experience, but the vacuum will also want the base station lugged up or down the stairs too). The suction is also a mystery; Shark has declined to comment on the exact suction. Still, we’ve loved low-suction vacuums before, and the results have been great.

This vacuum is one I refuse to part with, and while its retail price is technically $800, it's on sale enough in the $500 range that this has become the budget pick I'd easily recommend when it's on sale. The Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro is the newest update to Roborock's more affordable Qrevo line, which went without updates for years. The Qrevo 2 Pro is cheaper than the Curv 2 that launched in January 2026, and it still packs a ton of power, great navigation, and the same handy app. It comes with 20,000 Pa of suction, a FlexiArm mop that does a better job of corner cleaning, and a reversible side brush to help dislodge corner debris. I love seeing the arm reach out and get all the edges and corners around my house, especially underneath cabinets in the kitchen and bathroom.

The Qrevo 2 Pro also pulled ahead in some areas when compared against the similarly often-on-sale Eufy Omni C28. While the Eufy got itself stuck on cords in my bedroom, the Qrevo 2 Pro only attempted to eat cords without actually getting stuck on them. The Qrevo still isn't great at seeing small objects; it took my cat's toys for rides around the room, but they usually didn't get stuck or stop the vacuum. Both vacuums scored a 2 out of 3 on my Cheerio test, but the Qrevo 2 Pro got the harder fridge Cheerio with its FlexiArm mop. The Eufy did a little better on mopping, but neither vacuum did perfectly. I'm giving the Qrevo 2 Pro a 1.25 out of 2—one spill was just about gone, but the area around it was all slightly sticky, while the second spill was only half cleaned. It's hard to grade perfectly. It also occasionally leaves a little debris behind when it goes over thresholds that separate carpet from hard flooring, but it didn't have this concern when transitioning onto rugs.

According to recent reports, this vacuum (and its base station) also looks good and is fairly quiet. (Except when it cleans on tile, which is a noisy experience as it travels across the grout divots. But it does a good job.) Both the base station and vacuum itself are quieter than the Eufy Omni C28, and it is especially pleasant if you let the Qrevo 2 Pro vacuum and mop separately. It takes longer than doing the combo cleans, but this vacuum pulled off doing both a separate vacuuming session and mopping of my massive first floor in two hours, which most vacuums still take for combo cleans.

We've loved the app and navigation from Roborock for years, and it still stands out among its rivals in this area. The Roborock only struggles to navigate on a C-shaped table with long, thin, flat legs it can't see against my wood floors. Besides that it does a fantastic job navigating around all kinds of furniture and never runs into anything the way I've seen more expensive vacuums do. It can map multiple floors of my house too. Ultimately, it's a great, well-rounded vacuum for the price.

If the Roborock Qrevo isn't on sale, this Eufy is the next best thing. Former WIRED editor Adrienne So previously recommended Eufy’s older X10 Pro Omni as a great robot vacuum without spending too much, and Eufy released the Eufy Omni C28 in February this year with a similar set of features and price point. The Omni C28 comes with nearly double the suction power of the older model, a self-cleaning roller mop instead of mop pads, and retractable detangling brushes.

It does a solid job mopping and vacuuming, but it has a shorter battery life, leaving it at only 37 percent after completing the four-room main floor of my house. This is a bit of a bummer, since this affordable vacuum can do multi-floor mapping. While it can store enough maps to clean all three levels of my home, it doesn’t have the battery life to do so. But it does charge fairly quickly, and I was able to still clean all three floors of my house in a single day—I just had to let it recharge a little at the base first. It went back up to 57 percent battery life after just 20 minutes in its docking station. It also tried to eat the cords near my bed, and luckily I was nearby to yank them free. If you get this vacuum, make sure your cords are clear of the vacuum's reach.

With my corner Cheerio test, this vacuum also got two out of three Cheerios, but it missed the trickier fridge-corner Cheerio. This is the hardest spot to get into, so I’m not surprised, but it does mean you’ll have to check those corners more with this vacuum. The cherry juice spill test also showed similar results: The first spot it reached was cleaned completely, while the second spot, which had more time to dry, still had some sticky residue left behind.

Overall, though, it’s a good vacuum for the price, especially since it packs multi-floor mapping, the capability to mop and vacuum, and good results all around for a vacuum that’s already usually on sale for around or under $500.

Industry observers note that there are a lot of great robot vacuums out there. Here are a few others we’ve tried and liked.

Dreame L60 Ultra for $1,000: This vacuum did a good all-around job and packs a ton of good features, including dual flex arms, the EasyLeap System that lets it move over almost-2-inch tall obstacles, and 35,000 Pa of suction. This is a great one to buy if you have tall thresholds in your home thanks to that lifting feature, but otherwise, you could get a smarter vacuum for a cheaper price. This vacuum does promise dirt detection, but I never noticed it delivering on that promise. Still, my Dreame long-term tester commented that it's leagues quieter than her older Dreame vacuum, so it's a good upgrade choice if you like Dreame and want something quieter.

Dreame X50 Ultra for $800: If you have pets that tend to make one area of your home particularly hair- or debris-covered, this is the vacuum to get. The Dreame X50 Ultra has tons of great features, including double-roll brushes, side wands for edge cleaning, and a large-capacity docking station, but the real standout is the AI that can notice extremely dirty areas. It’s the most effective dirt- and obstacle-identification system that former WIRED editor Adrienne So has tried, and it will even remind her which areas it needs to clean more often (for her, that’s near her dog’s bed).

Dyson Spot+Scrub Ai for $800: The Dyson Spot+Scrub Ai is a good robot vacuum overall, with a unique base station design that calls back to the Dyson stick vacuums and built-in AI to find spots and stains on your floor to scrub them away. It mostly worked, but I did prefer this feature in the Shark above, which has a similar starting retail price but is usually on sale. It’s also a little tall, so if you have builder-grade cabinets like I do, it might not be able to vacuum the toe kicks or underneath your Ikea furniture. (It got stuck underneath my Tolstad bed frame and was too tall to get underneath my Besta cabinet.).

According to recent reports, matic Robot Vacuum Bundle for $1,495: According to former WIRED editor Adrienne So, this vacuum is spectacular. It’s the only 10/10 rating she’s ever given a robot vacuum. Its six RGB infrared cameras do a great job making a 3D map, the single waste bag contains wet and dry debris, it does a great job cleaning toe kicks, and it was quiet enough to run without bothering So’s kids while they watched TV. That’s due to Matic’s lower suction power (only 3,200 Pa), but she didn’t notice any decrease in cleanliness as a result. It’s compact and square, giving it the ability to really get into corners. The only bummer is that it has expensive, proprietary waste bags. But those waste bags do have diaper salts, charcoal, and a HEPA filter, so you don’t have to replace the filters separately.

Narwal Flow for $849: WIRED’s Reviews team hasn’t always had success with Narwal’s vacuums, but when I tested this model late last year, I found it super easy to set up and get cleaning. I had no connectivity complications, installation was a breeze, and the app was easy to navigate. It did a good job cleaning my hard floors and rug, and even when I ran it right out of the box until it ran out of battery, it returned itself to its station to recharge and then resumed the task a few hours later, all on its own. The base station is also sleek and cute compared with the dark, bulky structures most have.

In a recent development, roborock Saros 20 Flow for $1,300: If you're looking for something with serious suction, the Saros 20 Flow is my preferred choice out of Roborock's higher-power Saros line. I really like using it, and the roller mop does a good job mopping, but it only got one out of three Cheerios on my corner test and didn't manage to spot any stains on my floor, even with the promised built-in stain detection. It's the option I'd choose if you want a robot vacuum with great navigation and super-high suction (36,000 Pa) that won't deposit debris around the house like the Saros 20 tended to, but I think you'd be just as happy with a cheaper Roborock.

Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 for $1,000: This is another great option from Roborock and another part of the Qrevo line we've liked for years. The Qrevo Curv 2 came out in January and has similar strengths to the Qrevo 2 Pro above, but it has a roller mop called SpiraFlow instead of two individual mop pads. It also has similar struggles, with threshold debris and small objects being hard to spot. It's a good vacuum overall, and best on sale (which it often is!), but I'd pick my picks on sale over it.

In a recent development, A robot vacuum is an automated vacuum, usually shaped like a round disc, that moves around your house to vacuum (and mop, as many models these days include mopping) on your behalf. You might’ve heard some refer to these devices as “Roombas,” which is the brand that made the concept popular, but today just about every cleaning brand—from high-end Dyson to affordable Bissell—makes some kind of robot vacuum. They come with either a charging station or a larger docking station that can self-empty.

There are a few things most robot vacuums will need to work properly:.

The Federal Communications Commission declared in late July that foreign-produced advanced robotic devices will now be included on the FCC’s Covered List. That list includes communications equipment and services that are deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States—including robot vacuums (and similar devices like robotic pool cleaners and lawn mowers). While it won’t ban any models already on the market that have FCC approval, we’ll likely see a huge decline in available fresh models after this year. Models made in the US will be fine, but future vacuums from popular brands like Dreame, Eufy, Roborock, and more could be affected. For now, you'll still see vacuums launching from these brands, though, since FCC approval is given months ahead of product launches.

This decision comes from an interagency body in the White House executive branch called the National Security Determination, which has deemed automated robotic devices a security risk due to the data they collect, which could be used for surveillance and be remotely commandeered by “malign actors.” While the initial documentation describes humanoid robots and a recent case of a humanoid robot’s cybersecurity vulnerability to be remotely taken over, the official description of these robot devices will include robot vacuums and any devices meeting the following criteria:.

Overall, robot vacuums themselves aren’t banned, but new models from companies based outside the US won’t get FCC approval and can’t be sold in the US. You don’t need to stop using any robot vacuum you have, but if you’re in the market for a new one, it’s better to shop sooner before availability starts to decline—and prices are likely to rise as supply falls.

Dyson R3 Nurovi Spot+Scrub UV for $1,200: Dyson's newest version of the Spot+Scrub has a UV light to help its AI spot stains, and I was happy to see those stains reported in the app, but I couldn't tell if the vacuum actually did more detailed cleaning in those areas. That aside, I wanted to love this vacuum more than I did. My issue with the vacuum is how it did in regular cleaning sessions: It left pieces of popcorn behind when vacuuming on my downstairs rugs, didn't seem to ever get close enough to my walls for any kind of edge cleaning, and was too tall to get underneath cabinets or basic Ikea furniture around my house (but still smacked into that furniture over and over again due to camera placement). It also got a zero on my corner Cheerio test, failing to even get the Cheerio that just sits near a chair leg. I haven't tested either of the cheaper new Dyson robot vacuum options, but if this is how the best one does, I'm not inclined to.

Sources indicate that eufy S2 for $950: This robot vacuum has an intense-looking base station. However, I was disappointed it missed both the fridge and bookshelf Cheerios in my corner test, giving it only a one out of three. Both cherry stains were scrubbed away, but the floor near where the stains were felt sticky all over even with the stains ostensibly wiped away. It’s especially a bummer given the price point; it needed to do better to be worth such a high price tag.

iRobot Roomba Max 705 Combo for $800: The name Roomba is synonymous with robot vacuums for many people, but it’s actually a specific line made by iRobot. I really liked both the high-end look of the Max 705 Combo (not to be confused with the cheaper Max 705) and the overall job it did mopping and cleaning my floors. The app is great since it shows you a map of where the robot went, and it’ll also show you a little itinerary of which rooms it’s doing in what order. However, setup and any resetting you need to do is a long process, so be ready to commit and troubleshoot when you unbox it. My long-term tester has also reported that its mopping abilities have not improved over the six months it's been running in her house, but it does best with vacuuming and carpet.

iRobot Roomba Max 875 Combo With ThermaMist for $799: As Roomba’s new top-line robot vacuum and mop, this model features 35,000 Pa of suction, as well as hot steam to pretreat stuck-on stains. However, what really sold me was the “no pre-clean pickup” advertised on the box. I’ve got pet toys, my teen’s sports equipment and shoes all over the floor, cords, and loose rugs; other robot vacuums I’ve tried have struggled with my household. The Max 875, however, moved through my house with ease—in fact, I was quite impressed with how well it powered through even the toughest robovac challenges, like shoelaces and a maze of tucked-in chairs around a table. It did fine on pedestrian stains on my LVP floors, like spilled coffee, but even with the ThermaMist and repeated returns to the scene, the 875 Combo couldn’t fully clean an area with dried wet cat food. Setup was also pretty buggy—I followed the manual, but the vacuum took off before I could add it to the app and map my house, trying to clean a random area on 14 percent battery life. It would then return to the dock station, charge for five minutes, and repeat this process for well over an hour. When I did get it connected to the app, it remarked it needed an patch but was unable to download it. I eventually got it to work by factory-resetting the machine and starting all over, but this process took more patience than I’d expect at this price point. —Kat Merck.

In a recent development, iRobot Roomba Plus 678 Combo Robot + AutoWash Dock for $599: Like its fancier sibling, the Max 875 above, the Plus 678 had a bit of a buggy setup process that required several attempts and a factory reset. The Plus 678 also has the Max 875’s AI-powered stain pretreatment (though without the ThermaMist steam) and 30,000 Pa of suction for Roomba’s latest “SealForce” technology, which lowers a skirt around carpets to suction deeper into the pile. I tested this with three different types of rugs—a regular-pile wool rug, a loose washable rug, and a low-pile faux fur rug. It did well on the first two, but failed on the third, becoming fully stuck. (Most vacuums can’t handle this rug, so I don’t exactly fault it for this.) Other than the setup mishaps—which included false “brush roller failure” messages and a mapping attempt that left it turning around in circles in the middle of an open room for 20 minutes—this is a serviceable mop-vac with a feature list that’s hard to fault at this price. —Kat Merck.

iRobot Roomba Plus 575 Combo Robot + AutoWash Dock for $499: After hearing about the futuristic Roomba growing up, I was excited to see one in action. During setup, I found that the battery cover unscrewed, but assumed it was intentional since no screws were included. It soon fell off, so I taped it; days later, it came off during cleaning and got lost, leaving the battery and cords exposed to debris and the wet mop. Not great. From the start, it struggled to map my home. Cleaning requires app routines, which I didn’t love, as sometimes I just wanted to be able to click a single room and go without having to create another routine. The routines were often ignored or stopped midway. A mop pad fell off on every single run, forcing me to retrace the machine’s path to find it in my home. It also got caught on cords and repeatedly tried to climb my cat tree’s base, getting stuck perpetually spinning until I had to manually move it. Edge cleaning was nonexistent; there was so much cat hair and dust near where the floor met the wall. After a month, it threw up and scattered debris whenever it crossed the ¾-inch thresholds to the bathroom, kitchen, and bedroom, so afterward I had to vacuum the mess it created—defeating the purpose. —Molly Higgins.

According to recent reports, mova P10 Pro Ultra Gen2 for $360: This robot vacuum was solid, and especially did a good job with cleaning corners (it got a 2 out of 3 on the corner test, capturing both the stool and fridge Cheerios), but it did a poor job scrubbing away the cherry juice for my stain tests. One of the two stains was almost entirely left behind, and overall on casual runs of the vacuum it didn’t feel as if my floors were super clean. Still, if you’re looking for good corner cleaning, and carpets more than hard-floor deep cleaning, this is a solid robot vacuum for the price.

Recent findings suggest that roborock Saros 20 for $990: WIRED reviewer Adrienne So was mostly happy with this robot vacuum, as was I. She noticed the super-high suction (it hits 36,000 Pa) actually caused more debris to be left behind on her hard floors when it passed over thresholds; I didn't have this issue with the thresholds in my home, but instead I found debris on my hard floors immediately after having this vacuum clean them, with no threshold required. It also only got a one out of three in my Cheerio test, which isn't great for such an expensive vacuum.

Tapo RV50 Pro Omni for $400: After testing several robovacs that made me want to chuck them out the window, I had high hopes for Tapo’s latest model that was released this summer. It promised over four hours of run time, dual-laser obstacle avoidance, DeepEdge mopping for corners and edges, and automatic floor detection to keep mops off carpets. But during more than two weeks of testing, it never mapped my home correctly or fully cleaned it. It couldn’t cross the ¾-inch raised thresholds into my kitchen or bathroom, and it mapped my bedroom but detected a phantom obstacle and cleaned only the 2-foot entryway. My kitchen, bathroom, and bedroom were never fully cleaned during testing. It’d be heading for the dock to wash mops or empty them and would forget to do the hall next or finish the living room and begin charging again. About half the time, the app asked me to map my home again, apparently forgetting the previous day’s map. During mapping, it sometimes started cleaning, got lost, and then confirmed it couldn’t find its dock, leaving me to locate and return it. When vacuuming, it sometimes left the mops at the station, returned for them, forgot, and began charging, thus ending its task. Not once did it successfully vacuum and mop my whole home. Online reviews are glowing, so perhaps I got a dud—but this experience was enough to make me want to clean by hand instead. —Molly Higgins.

Industry observers note that I test all robot vacuums in my three-story townhouse, where they clean across luxury vinyl plank (LVP); tile; carpet; and a large, low-pile rug. I have a dining table and four barstools to navigate, and both a cat and a child who create daily messes. I run the vacuum at least three times across the main floors of my home to assess its overall performance and note any recurring concerns or errors it encounters. I do pick up my son’s toys, but I like to watch how the robot navigates the various chair legs and side tables throughout my home, and whether it sucks up the power cords beside my bed. I also like to see how much battery life is left after a run is complete on each level of my home.

My corner test, using three Cheerios in three corner (or cornerlike) spots.

Sources indicate that I also set up an obstacle course of sorts. The first one is the corner test, created by three Cheerios placed in three tricky corners on the middle floor of my home: one in the corner of an Ikea Billy bookshelf toe kick, one underneath my countertops next to the fridge, and one next to a barstool chair leg. It’s how I test how well each robot vacuum gets into corners and underneath cabinetry.

My spill test, with two spots of cherry juice on the floor.

According to recent reports, I also create intentional spills for these vacuums to clean up. I use maraschino cherry juice to create two spill spots, then use a paper towel to smear and thin the stain to better replicate a spill you might not have seen on your floors. Many robot vacuums have AI that promises to detect these kinds of stains, but so far, no vacuum has stopped and scrubbed both spots on its first try.

Can You Use Robot Vacuums on All Kinds of Floors?

You can, especially since there are so many mopping models now to better clean hard flooring. You can use these devices on anything from hardwood to LVP and tile, though I wouldn't recommend leaving smaller rugs out for these autonomous gadgets to get stuck on. Large, set rugs are fine, but bathroom and kitchen mats or any thin, easily moved rugs should be cleared out of the way and put in the wash instead of vacuumed by your robot vac.

How Often Do You Need to Maintain Your Robot Vacuum?

Taking good care of your robot vacuum will help it last. Here’s the debris-removal process you should follow for each robot vacuum style.

Make sure to review your robot vacuum’s manual for any other steps the manufacturer recommends you take regularly to keep the vacuum running for as long as possible. Many brands also have replacement parts, so you can swap out individual pieces like brushes without needing an entirely new vacuum.

Do I Still Need a Regular Vacuum if I Have a Robot Vacuum?

I recommend keeping some kind of vacuum on hand, though that can vary based on your home. If you have stairs, you’ll definitely still want a hand vacuum or stick vacuum that can easily maneuver and clean your staircase, while pet owners might want a vacuum that can clean upholstery. I prefer my Dyson stick vacuums for a good carpet clean, but your mileage may vary depending on your preferences. Either way, I think everyone needs a companion vacuum of some kind with a robot vacuum.

Do You Need a Self-Emptying Dock?

You don’t need it, but a self-emptying dock makes using a robot vacuum much easier. You aren’t fumbling with debris every time it runs, and having a single bag to remove or a bin to empty is much easier than pulling debris out of the vacuum itself. I’d even recommend choosing a stick vac with a self-emptying dock, as it just makes the whole experience so much easier.

How Does WIRED Obtain Robot Vacuums? What Happens When We’re Done Testing?

Almost all the robot vacuums we test are provided to us as press samples with the understanding that there is no guarantee of coverage or type of coverage. Most companies don’t want a used vacuum back, so we either donate them locally or have the top performers long-term tested to see how they last.

In 2021, before Oasis Security was even founded, I sat down with co-founder Danny Brickman and came away thinking he had something familiar. He showed the same drive weâd seen in the founders of two other Sequoia companies, Wiz and Cyera, whose founders, like Danny, had come up through Talpiot, the leadership program of the IDF. I wrote about that meeting a couple of years later in my investment memo, when we backed Oasis Security, at the Series A. I didnât realize at the time how literally connected that comparison would turn out to be. Today, Oasis is joining Cyera â and it turns out the foundersâ stories make the case for this combination almost as well as the technology does.

Three years ago, the pitch for Oasis was simple: enterprises were about to have far more machine identities than human ones, and almost nobody had a real way to manage or secure them. That was true then. Itâs far more true now. Every AI agent creates or uses non-human identities â API keys, service accounts, OAuth tokens, agent-to-agent credentials â that act with real permissions and real blast radius, and that donât behave anything like the human identities the last generation of identity tooling was built around. AI drove non-human identity from a niche IAM subcategory to a board-level CISO conversation. Danny Brickman and his co-founder Amit Zimerman built Oasis, which they call agentic access management, for exactly that world.

Sources indicate that cyera arrived at the same shift from a different direction. Yotam Segev, Tamar Bar-Ilan, and Yonatan Itai built the organization to answer a deceptively simple question: where does an organizationâs sensitive data actually live, who can reach it, and whatâs really at risk? As AI agents started reading, writing and acting on that data, they reached a conclusion that now looks obvious: securing AI means securing the data, the identities acting on it (human and non-human), and the agents themselves.

Put the two products side by side, and they complement each other perfectly. Cyera knows where the sensitive data is. Oasis knows who or what can actually touch it â every service account, API key and agent credential, and whether itâs behaving the way it should. Itâs a bit like a bank vault: the best way to protect it is by knowing both whatâs inside and whoâs approaching. Data security tells you whatâs actually at stake. Identity security tells you whether the thing touching your data is legitimate. Together, the two products cover the entire path an AI agent takes through a companyâs environment, from the data it touches to the identity it uses to touch it.

Thereâs a practical case here too. Cyera has built one of the most powerful enterprise GTM teams, with the kind of scale that usually takes a startup a decade to reach. Oasisâs product now gets to run through that engine, into enterprise accounts it would otherwise have taken years to earn on its own. And the market isnât waiting: Whoever builds the first genuinely complete AI security platform, spanning data, identity and agents, has a real shot at becoming the default layer enterprises standardize on as agentic AI rolls out. Speed and completeness both matter, and the combination of Cyera and Oasis creates both.

The foundersâ backgrounds make the fit feel almost inevitable in hindsight. Itâs a small world: two teams weâd backed independently, drawn from the same pool of Israeli technical talent, ended up building the two halves of the same answer to AI security. Talpiot and Unit 8200 alumni have produced a disproportionate share of the last decadeâs big cybersecurity companies, so the coincidence is smaller than it looks, but itâs still a good sign when it plays out this cleanly.

Recent findings suggest that danny, Amit and the Oasis team built the category-defining firm in non-human identity in under three years, from a standing start to a product enterprises trust with agentic access at scale. That doesnât happen without genuinely hard technical work, and a founder team that saw the shift to agentic AI before almost anyone else in security did. We at Sequoia have backed both Cyera and Oasis since their Series A rounds, and weâre proud to keep backing this team as they take on the next chapter together â a bigger stage, and an opportunity sized to match.

Meta Refused to Share Muse for Testing, UK Financial Watchdog Complains

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (520 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that meta declined a suggestion from the UK’s financial regulator last week that they joint-test Muse using their sandbox, according to the watchdog’s head of innovation Colin Payne.
  • “It’s another force of attack, agents hitting the streets, most of them coming from the US,” Payne, of the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), mentioned Tuesday in a panel hosted by AI firm Whitespace.
  • His organization has been experimenting with other firms as many, including Amazon, roll out AI shopping assistants, and other agentic tools in the UK.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that meta declined a suggestion from the UK’s financial regulator last week that they joint-test Muse using their sandbox, according to the watchdog’s head of innovation Colin Payne. It comes as regulators across the UK, including the competition and data watchdogs, warned Meta it needs to ensure its AI products comply with UK consumer protection laws.

“It’s another force of attack, agents hitting the streets, most of them coming from the US,” Payne, of the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA), mentioned Tuesday in a panel hosted by AI firm Whitespace. “We’ve got a number of entrants into the market. We want to see what they’re going to be doing in the market. I think it’s just reasonable,” he later explained to WIRED. Payne told WIRED the FCA had been hoping the organizations could work together to investigate what interactions might look like between the tool, marketed as a personal assistant, and a normal customer.

His organization has been experimenting with other firms as many, including Amazon, roll out AI shopping assistants, and other agentic tools in the UK.

The FCA especially wants to understand how payments will be made by agents—as multiple British retailers, including grocers Sainsbury’s, Marks & Spencer, and Ocado, department store Debenhams Group, and electronics seller Currys stated they’d been working with Meta to smooth Muse’s access to their sites. Payne is concerned about potential unintended consequences of prompts, especially when a user has a low level of understanding of how the AI product works. “If an agent is acting autonomously, we want to make sure it’s in the interest of the consumer,” he notes.

Payne did note the testing would have taken time to set up. “Normally you have a long period of time speaking to a firm and then you plan it over a period of weeks or months,” he explained, but Meta only made the FCA aware of its plans last month.

“We’ve engaged constructively with the appropriate regulatory authorities and will continue to do so,” Meta Spokesperson Matthew Pollard tells WIRED.

More than 10 million consumers have set up Muse in North America since it was launched in September. British watchdogs say they will be monitoring Muse’s rollout closely as they are bracing for significant uptake on their side of the pond, too, given that many Brits already use Meta’s other products, like Instagram, Facebook, and WhatsApp. “If it’s going to be equally popular in the UK, we need to be able to see what it’s going to do,” Payne claims.

Sources indicate that the ICO stressed the importance of users understanding and being able to control how Muse uses their personal data. The Competition and Markets Authority has already made Meta adapt its terms and conditions for UK consumers to say Meta must exercise “reasonable skill and care/professional diligence” when providing Muse, the EU and UK terms say, with the document acknowledging that outputs may still be inaccurate and actions may not be completed as intended.

“If we have concerns, we will not hesitate to act to protect UK consumers,” the CMA noted in a statement.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alon and team are training a foundation model for defensive cybersecurity, for enterprises to defend themselves against AIâs scaling offensive capabilities.

Alon and team are training a foundation model for defensive cybersecurity, for enterprises to defend themselves against AIâs scaling offensive capabilities.

Sources indicate that cybersecurity is a perpetual fight between the good guys and the bad. The age of agentic AI and Mythos-class models has tipped the scales in favor of the bad guys, opening a Pandoraâs box for offensive capabilities. An explosion in CVEs has since ensued.

Cyberattacks are about technical exploitation, which requires coding and reasoning prowess. Anthropicâs Mythos can discover and exploit zero-day vulnerabilities. Any model paired with a harness brings the cost of social engineering attacks down to near zero, unleashing them at unprecedented scale. The danger is heightened with every new model release.

Defensive security isnât improving in parallel. The relevant data lives in logs, events, traces and telemetry, a fundamentally different modality than the bodies of text LLMs usually train on, which barely show up in pretraining. Unlike offensive cybersecurity, which involves goal-directed reasoning towards a defined objective, defense requires open-ended reasoning, continually finding anomalies across vast amounts of normal-looking activity, a distinct capability that typically demands extensive domain-specific training. In short, defense is out of distribution for general-purpose frontier models: neither the data nor the intuition it requires is well-represented in training. In the race toward AGI, we cannot expect the frontier labs to take the detour of overhauling their training pipelines for defensive cybersecurity. And we certainly canât afford to bet our security on a hope that they do.

Corma has illustrated this âdefense gapâ in testing. They ran red/blue team simulations where an attacker plants a hidden backdoor and a defender tries to find it. The defender failed to find the backdoor 78% of the time, even when the defender was an identical copy of the very same model that planted it. Holding model quality constant, attackers will always have an advantage.

According to recent reports, the only answer to scaling laws on offense is better scaling laws on defense. Recent events have shown that frontier AI for defensive cybersecurity is one of the crucial unsolved problems of the AI age. Solving it is the generational mission Corma was founded on.

Corma founder and CEO Alon Pluda and his team are training a foundation model to power defensive cybersecurity agents. Cybersecurity, like Go or chess, is a two-player, zero-sum game with a clean reward (were you breached or not?) and an endless supply of games to play. Reinforcement learning and self-play have produced superhuman results before in this kind of paradigm. We are seeing history repeat itself. Corma pushes this further with large-scale reinforcement learning across cybersecurity environments that replicate real enterprise networks, with all their tools, telemetry and noise â as part of a training pipeline that produces frontier defensive capabilities, outperforming general-purpose foundation models, with much lower per-token inference costs.

In the cat-and-mouse game of cybersecurity, we believe Cormaâs vertical integration and âsovereign AIâ approach will win. Cost matters (always-on inference costs can rack up rapidly). Owning the model weights matters (they arenât subject to restrictions on cybersecurity-related usage set by the closed model labs). And specialization and inference speed really matter (fastest to protect against a new threat wins).

Cormaâs foundation model is deployed and productized as an agentic Security Workforce. These workers operate across different security tools and take on roles spanning the entire security organization: from security operations and identity management to cloud and network security and beyond. They are on the job at Fortune 500 companies and large enterprises across healthcare, finance, critical infrastructure, retail and more.

Cormaâs foundation model powers agents that complete defensive work end to end. We spoke to one CISO whose Corma agent notified him of a pending attack through his Garmin watch while he was on a walk with his dog in the evening; with one confirmation, the agent was able to shut the attacker down, all while he was still walking. In another instance, within its first hour on the job, Corma uncovered, contained and remediated an active attacker campaign inside a customerâs network that their security team had missed for 52 days.

It has been revealed that training frontier foundation models for defensive cybersecurity requires world-class hackers and world-class researchers â almost no company on earth has both. Alon is personally one of the most elite hackers in the world, and has assembled a cohesive and interdisciplinary team of hackers and researchers that is hill-climbing on technical challenges and building impressive commercial momentum.

We are thrilled to lead Cormaâs seed round and to be their partner as they chart latest territory in what is sure to be one of the most dynamic races in AI.

#38071. Thuma Dupes: Japanese Joinery Bed Frames That Stack Up (2026)

📅 10 Sep 2025 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2401 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Thuma Dupes: Japanese Joinery Bed Frames That Stack Up (2026)

📅 10 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2401 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Japanese joinery bed frames are bolt-free beds made from notched wood pieces that slide and click together to make a stable frame.
  • Thuma is the leading brand in this space, and we love its product lineup—several members of the WIRED Reviews team have tested Thuma beds, and all rave about them.
  • Japanese joinery is a traditional carpentry method that uses only wooden components.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Silk & Snow (queen, with solid headboard).

Japanese joinery bed frames are bolt-free beds made from notched wood pieces that slide and click together to make a stable frame. Think Jenga, but with really nice, sleek wooden furniture. The advantages are many, starting with easy assembly that takes just a few minutes and requires no tools.

Thuma is the leading brand in this space, and we love its product lineup—several members of the WIRED Reviews team have tested Thuma beds, and all rave about them. However, they’re not cheap. A Thuma bed frame starts at $895 for a twin frame with no headboard, and the king-sized Thuma signature bed our testers loved costs $2,500.

Japanese joinery is a traditional carpentry method that uses only wooden components. Instead of nailing boards together, each piece of wood is carved so it snugly fits into openings carved into neighboring pieces—the “joints,” if you will. The tension and strong hold of the interconnected pieces create structural integrity.

It has been revealed that it’s a pretty easy way to channel your inner Bob the Builder, and the finished bed frame looks stunning in its simplicity. However, we are always on the lookout for products at the intersection of high quality and low price—curious to see if any contenders could give Thuma a run for its money—so we researched and tested, and these are our findings.

Be sure also to check out our guides on the best mattresses we’ve tested, as well as the best pillows and bedsheets. You’ll need something to put on your new frame, after all!

Updated November 2026: We’ve added two newly introduced bed frames to this guide and ensured accuracy throughout.

DreamCloud (queen, with bamboo headboard).

I’m a longtime fan of DreamCloud mattresses, so it came as no surprise that the brand’s Japanese joinery bed frame is excellent. Like the mattress, this frame has numerous thoughtful details that stood out immediately.

DreamCloud made setup seamless. Each piece is labeled, and when it comes time to put it all together, take a gander at the endpoints of the long pieces. If you look closely at the joints where they intersect at the ends, you will see holes drilled into the top and bottom pieces. Small rods attach to the boards and fit into them, serving as a secondary mechanism to ensure stability. I find this impressive because the beams stack neatly into the grooves carved into the ends. In a word, it’s crisp. It’s a tiny detail, but the frame stayed virtually silent when I put a mattress on it or moved around in my sleep. I didn’t notice any shaking, either.

Industry observers note that another excellent feature is the frame’s center stability beam (crucial for preventing long-term sagging), which slides in last. This lets you avoid nesting it before closing the frame, unlike some other Japanese joinery models from different brands. It’s far more convenient.

Lining up the slats is the most challenging part of the process; you have to make sure everything is aligned perfectly. To help the process go smoothly, you’ll find wooden rods—similar to those on the ends of the boards—in the center of the bed, where you insert the slatted frames. They’re about the width of a pencil. Pop those slats in, unroll, Velcro to keep in place, and go.

Sources indicate that you don’t need a headboard with this frame, but DreamCloud provided one for testing. Two square openings are located inside the top beam of the frame, right where your head would be. The headboard slides into these internal slots, which hold the end pieces and keep it upright. Foam block stickers are included to be attached last, so your wall doesn’t get scuffed up. All that, and still no tools necessary. Down to the details, people! And this detail you don’t want to skip—it’s around $449 for a queen. The headboard costs $299 extra, but even with that, it’s still far cheaper than luxury alternatives. You’ll also have two stain options: natural or a very pretty walnut.

It has been revealed that that stated, you’ll have to consider how many sleepers will use this frame and the weight of the mattress you’ll place on it. When I was testing new mattresses every week, two of the frame’s center support legs split right down the middle. Make sure you don’t screw them on too tightly, as I suspect the tension is what made the wood look like I had been chopping it with a small axe. Regardless, I was shocked to see this happen, and it is another notch on Thuma’s belt for heightened durability. —Julia Forbes.

The Bamboo Bed Frame by DreamCloud ranges from $299 for a twin to $549 for a California king (frame only).

Silk & Snow (queen, with solid headboard).

Industry observers note that silk & Snow is another brand that I hold in high regard. Every time I’ve tested a mattress from the brand, it consistently packs quality for the price. This platform bed frame was no exception. There are two options: natural rubberwood and acacia wood. I opted for the latter, which is a medium-brown color. I thought that the stain was stunning, with a richness akin to a lovely latte. However, I really appreciate that they offer options not just in wood stain color, but also in the actual hardwood itself.

This frame arrived in four separate boxes. I liked this approach because it protected the wood stain’s integrity during shipping. Every other frame in this guide was packed into one box—not unlike a mattress-in-a-box, but heavier and longer. I actually preferred this route, as every box was also labeled for easy setup.

Like the DreamCloud frame, Silk & Snow’s doesn’t require tools or hardware to set up—it’s made entirely of wood. One thing I learned the hard way: Make sure the center beam is within the frame perimeter before fully closing it off. Then place the slats into the internal notches on the side rails, and it’s ready for a mattress. I had no issues with noise, shaking, or feeling unstable. It supported a mattress just fine, and I am still truly enamored with how the wood stain looked amidst my studio’s decor.

Sources indicate that however, I do a lot of testing, so I’m constantly setting up and taking down mattresses, frames, and bedding. This is where having two people will be crucial, as I decided to do it all by myself for the sake of time, to the detriment of the frame. The frame got badly scratched up around the slatted portions where the corners of the boards stack together, due to my awkward solo assembly motions. I doubt you’ll be doing this as much as I do, but it was still a bit disappointing to see. Despite this, it’s worth recommending because I loved how it looked and performed. —Julia Forbes.

The Silk & Snow Wooden Platform bed frame ranges from $550 for a twin to $900 for a king (frame only).

Sources indicate that the Avocado City Bed Frame is a minimalist wood (blonde or walnut) platform frame with a completely tool-free Japanese-joinery assembly process. The same natural, nontoxic, and sustainable materials practices that guide the company’s mattresses are at play here as well.

Recent findings suggest that the City Bed is regularly $1,299 for a queen, and it is the most affordable of Avocado’s bed options (though you have to factor in a shipping fee). It’s made from very nice, solid wood (I tested the walnut version). There’s an optional headboard that I did not test. The bed itself is attractive, fairly subtle, and unobtrusive. In fact, if your duvet is reasonably large, you may not even see much of the bedframe.

Sources indicate that the frame fits together using interlocking joints with metal reinforcements. In my testing, it’s been solid and sturdy, with no squeaking or any signs of weak joints. It is a tight fit at times, especially at the four corners, and I had to tap it with a soft mallet to get it fully flush (which sort of defeats the no-tool promise, but you probably could have done the same with a copy of Infinite Jest or something equally solid). —Scott Gilbertson.

The Avocado City bed frame ranges from $750 for a twin to $1,499 for a California king (frame only).

Sources indicate that the Birch frame was the most basic of the Thuma dupes I tested. I was really excited about this one because the wood is sourced from the land of the pines, otherwise known as my home state of North Carolina. Poplar is a durable hardwood, and southern yellow pine is one of the harder pine woods. (I can attest to this because, for an eighth-grade science project, I tested the durability of regional woods.) The manufacturing partner is a certified member of the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC). The legs are made of a completely different wood, Appalachian maple. It also uses a soy-based resin to remain completely formaldehyde-free.

Sources indicate that it arrived in two boxes, and setup was quick and easy—the step-by-step instructions were the most thorough of the bunch. With written descriptions and pictures, it’s hard to mess this up. Plus, you don’t need any tools to get this frame up and running. The outer boards were polished to maintain the gorgeous hue of the pine wood. However, be cautious when handling the inner slatted-board sections, as this wood is not finished. I got a small splinter and was not a happy camper. Next, I set up the bed and slept on it for a week—the standard amount of time I test mattresses. The first few days, this thing creaked and moaned like crazy. It didn’t feel stable, and I was shaken if I moved even slightly. By the end of the week, it seemed to fall into place and settle, so I no longer noticed the noise or motion.

I don’t want to discount this as a possible option, though, because the wood quality was what I wanted it to be, and so was the overall price. If you’re looking for a cheaper option for a guest room, upgrading your teen’s room, or furnishing a first apartment on a budget, this could work well for you. —Julia Forbes.

The Birch Madison bed frame ranges from $749 for a twin to $978 for a California king.

Nectar Sleep (queen, frame only).

Nectar Sleep (queen, with bamboo headboard).

It has been revealed that I had never set up or slept on a Japanese joinery-style bed frame before testing this model from Nectar, and now I’m a true believer. The frame is made from bamboo, and assembly took just about 20 minutes with no tools required.

Putting it together was super simple: the four feet had cut-out notches where the frame slid into place, and you just needed to push down to make the pieces lock together—it’s essentially like putting together a giant set of Lincoln Logs. After sliding the footboard into the feet’s notches, you finish both sides the same way by pushing down into the notches. The middle section is springy and has a floating foot to adjust for the bed’s pressure, so no cumbersome box spring is needed. The slats are connected with Velcro and just need to be unspooled and adhered to the sides. I opted for a headboard that slides in from above and stays in place because of the cutouts on the head portion of the frame below.

In a recent development, I’m physically disabled, so putting together furniture with tools and nails or screws is nearly impossible. I recommend that anyone who’s in a similar position check out a Japanese-style bed frame, as it’s lightweight, requires no additional tools, and requires very little physical strength. Plus, this frame comes in two colors, has optional headboard attachments, a 60-night home trial, a two-year warranty, and free shipping. —Molly Higgins.

The Nectar Bamboo bed frame ranges from $299 for a twin to $549 for a California king (frame only).

Here’s the thing: Thuma is still a Japanese joinery bed frame. Therefore, I’d be remiss not to include it on this list. While I can vouch that the options above are credible dupes, many of my teammates feel nothing beats the original in this case.

Thuma’s Classic Bed Frame is made from upcycled, sturdy rubberwood that comes in four finishes: walnut, natural, espresso, and gray. You can also choose different headboard variations, including all-wood, a pillow board (Italian wool and foam), or a hybrid of the two. The design’s not only beautiful, but it’s also backed by certifications such as UL GreenGuard Gold and CertiPur-US (if you opt for the pillow board).

WIRED Gear Editor Julian Chokkattu has had his Thuma frame for several years, and he notes it takes next to no time to set up. He also loves that it doesn’t creak or slide—just a strong sense of security while sleeping on it.

The Thuma Classic bed frame ranges from $895 for a twin to $1,495 for a California king (frame only).

It has been revealed that just like with the best mattresses we regularly test, each frame required a week of testing (not including naps) to evaluate night-over-night performance. This also allowed time for the frames to settle into place and perform alongside the bed each was paired with.

How Do I Set Up a Japanese Joinery Bed Frame?

Your bed frame should come with installation instructions, whether it features Japanese joinery construction or not. In the same vein, I recommend having someone assist you with the setup. As mentioned in our Silk & Snow review, this helps mitigate the risk of bumping and scratching your upcoming furniture.

Are These Bed Frames Better Than Thuma’s?

According to recent reports, we wouldn’t say better, just different. Each brand offers its own approach to creating a bed frame that adheres to the Japanese joinery method. This could include the type of wood used, the stains offered, the types of headboards you can pair it with, where it was manufactured, and, of course, the price.

#38069. Best Gaming Mouse (2026): My Picks After Testing Dozens of Mice
