Best Gaming Mouse (2026): My Picks After Testing Dozens of Mice

📅 17 Aug 2019 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4180 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Picking a gaming mouse can be difficult.
  • In a recent development, that’s why I take the time to test countless gaming mice—to tell you what works and what doesn’t.
  • Be sure to read our other peripheral buying guides for more, including the Best Ergonomic Mouse, Best Gaming Headsets, Best Mechanical Keyboards, and Best Hall Effect Keyboards.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Picking a gaming mouse can be difficult. There are countless metrics to factor in and a nearly unlimited number of mice with unique approaches in defining what's best. Quite honestly, it’s a market rife with opportunities for analysis paralysis to take hold.

In a recent development, that’s why I take the time to test countless gaming mice—to tell you what works and what doesn’t. I can’t say precisely which mouse will work for you—that’s dependent not only on technical specs but on your preferences, needs, budget, and hand size—but hopefully I can provide some insights into the top options out there, what's the best for specific types of gamers, and why I’ve picked them.

Be sure to read our other peripheral buying guides for more, including the Best Ergonomic Mouse, Best Gaming Headsets, Best Mechanical Keyboards, and Best Hall Effect Keyboards.

Updated November 2026: I've added the Razer Basilisk V4 Pro and Wallhack M-001. I've also included the Logitech G Pro X3 Superstrike in my honorable mentions, reorganized the list, and updated prices.

The Razer Cobra HyperSpeed (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is far more reasonable and practical than most of the ultra-light options today. Instead of shaving down features and mass to make the simplest mouse possible, the Cobra Hyperspeed finds an ideal middle ground, maintaining features like RGB lighting, Bluetooth connectivity, and options for wireless charging. Despite that, it still weighs below 70 grams, a number that was unbelievable for even the most premium wireless mice a decade ago. Inside, it’s packing an optical sensor, optical switches, and an optical scroll wheel—all top-of-the-line parts that are some of the fastest and most reliable on the market. While the mouse is limited to 1,000-Hz polling with the included low-profile USB-A dongle (which I prefer for convenience), it can be upgraded to 8,000 Hz with the bulkier and less-convenient HyperPolling dongle, cutting out its only serious limitation.

According to recent reports, beyond that, this mouse can do practically everything. It works as a travel mouse, a permanent desktop solution, and is even compatible with Razer’s wireless charging pucks, which lets you charge the mouse using either the Mouse Dock Pro, which ups your polling rate to 8,000 Hz, or the HyperFlux V2 wireless charging mousepad. The simple, symmetrical shape is comfortable and easy to hold, with the curved buttons on top creating spots to rest your fingers, while the low, gradual curve feels natural for resting your palm. Plus, its near-symmetry means it can be used as an ambidextrous mouse in a pinch (although lefties will miss out on the side buttons).

It has been revealed that while the price may be steep, Wallhack’s M-001 (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is one of the best I’ve tested in a long time. Although the specs aren’t quite cutting-edge (the sensor is a bit outdated, and some of the internals are still mechanical instead of optical), every aspect of this mouse’s user experience has been fine-tuned to perfection. That's what sets it apart for me.

The mouse itself is made entirely from magnesium, and the outer shell doesn’t feature any of the large weight-saving cutouts used by similar mice from Corsair, AngryMiao, and even Razer. Instead, the upper is entirely solid, and all of the cutouts are on the underside of the mouse. Because of this, the battery can be swapped out within seconds.

Alongside the mouse itself, the M-001’s dongle is one of the best on the market. Instead of simply sitting on a desk, this dongle incorporates physical dials to adjust the mouse’s sensitivity and polling rate, and recharges the spare battery when not in use.

In a recent development, while it may be silly, my favorite feature of this mouse is the swappable batteries themselves. Similar to a Nintendo Switch cartridge or an SD card, the batteries feature a push-lock mechanism that’s robust, satisfying, and intuitive, improving significantly on the magnet or rotation-lock systems that other swappable mouse batteries use.

In a recent development, the Rival 3 (7/10, WIRED Recommends) is a simple, no-frills gaming mouse. It’s lightweight, robust, and pretty much hits all the marks for gaming: Easy-access side buttons, clicky main buttons, underside RGB lighting, and a grippy rubberized scroll wheel. This SteelSeries mouse doesn’t innovate much, but like a Toyota Camry, it’s simple and reliable enough to get nearly anything done. At a price below $50, you’re getting all the performance you can realistically use for non-professional gaming. There aren’t any unnecessary features that add complication, and the mouse can be fully disassembled in under five minutes with a set of Phillips and Torx screwdrivers.

The Razer Viper V4 Pro (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is the latest installment in a long line of fantastic competitive mice, offering performance improvements across every metric. Along with top-of-the-line specs, optical sensors across the board, and a great symmetrical shape, the V4 also incorporates the same spherical dongle included with the Deathadder V4 Pro, which maintains its 8,000-Hz polling while adding LED indicators for information like connection quality, battery life, and DPI stage.

Sources indicate that using the exact same shape as the V3, this mouse is comfortable and intuitive to use. The shape is easy to move around, with small curves on the mouse buttons for your fingertips to rest, and the curvature of the sides creates natural spots for your thumb and pinky. The Razer Synapse software is one of the most powerful and intuitive on the market. There are customization options for mouse dpi, tracking distance, dynamic sensitivity, and even adjusting the mouse sensor to accommodate a rotated grip.

In a recent development, the only downside of the Viper V4 Pro is how uncompromising it is— there's no Bluetooth, and the included 2.4-GHz dongle requires a USB-A to USB-C cable (included) that runs to your computer, with no option for a smaller USB-A dongle (last seen on the V2). These decisions were made to lighten the mouse and improve connection quality, but they can be inconvenient if you need a wireless gaming mouse to pair with a laptop.

The Infinity .97 is one of the lightest mice I’ve tested at only 48.3 grams (without the removable rear panel, which adds 3.8 grams), and one of the sturdiest thanks to its magnesium upper shell. While the skeletal shape may look off-putting at first, it was far more comfortable and usable than I would have expected, especially when used with a fingertip grip. However, anyone dedicated to a palm or claw grip will likely be better served by a larger mouse with a sturdier back end.

Recent findings suggest that beyond weight, this mouse has fantastic specs: 8,000-Hz polling, optical switches, and a rating of 0.2 ms of latency all put it on par with Razer and Logitech’s best offerings. The most impressive feature by far is the removable and magnetically hot-swappable batteries that recharge using the mouse’s 2.4G dongle. This eliminates downtime from a dead battery and reduces the risks of long-term battery degradation and failure (assuming AngryMiao continues to sell spares).

Industry observers note that while the styling is certainly more of an acquired taste, the large gaps result in a shape that’s rigid and better-looking than the usual uniform, hexagon-shaped holes. The shape is shockingly comfortable despite the gaps (which are placed to preserve typical touch points), and the removable rear “hatchback” panel finds a reasonable balance between a standard shape and the ultra-lightweight “fingertip mice” that have become more popular in recent years.

Industry observers note that the software is also shockingly robust, with expected adjustments for DPI, polling, macros, and so on, alongside more granular adjustments like debounce speed, motion sync, ripple correction, and a Blast Mode that sets the mouse’s internal sensor to its maximum speed of 20,000 Hz. (It’s worth noting that the mouse still communicates with your computer at 8,000 Hz—this simply provides more data from the sensor to the mouse). Also, unlike some similarly-priced offerings, this mouse has both 2.4G and Bluetooth connectivity.

Industry observers note that the Basilisk V3 Pro was a fantastic mouse, and the V4 Pro significantly improves the technical specs while maintaining some of the best features. Primarily, the V4 Pro has an absurdly-high 8,000-Hz polling rate and a scroll wheel with smooth, ratcheted, and “high-sensitivity” scrolling options. This mouse also maintains the same four-button layout on the side, and has a larger shape with an integrated thumb rest for comfortable long-term use.

It has been revealed that as far as comfort and practicality, the Basilisk’s sculpted shape and thumb rest feel more like an office mouse than a gaming mouse, but the curved mouse buttons and smooth overall shape mean a claw grip still isn’t out of the question. The mouse wheel also has horizontal scrolling that’s activated by tilting it to the left or right, and the large number of programmable side buttons are great for both gaming and multimedia editing. While it’s still fairly hefty at 98 grams, this mouse is great if you’re either ambivalent about weight and want something more ergonomic, or if you prefer a heavier mouse. It might not be worth an upgrade when coming from the previous model, though, given the price.

The Pro X Superlight 2C is only marginally smaller than the standard Superlight 2, and weighs 51 grams, a 15 percent drop. It's essentially a scaled-down version. They are both capable of 8,000-Hz polling, use the same 44,000 dots-per-inch Hero 2 sensor, and have the same quoted 95-hour battery life. Because the 2C packs all this into a smaller package, it’s ideal for people with smaller hands, or anyone who primarily plays using a claw grip and doesn’t need the extra weight.

Recent findings suggest that it's not a travel-size mouse, but I think the 2C is better suited than most ultralight mice on this list. It uses a small USB-A dongle that can slot into a removable panel on the underside of the mouse for transport, and the shell is fairly sturdy. I wouldn’t toss it into a checked bag at the airport or wedge it into a side pocket, but it should hold up for light travel.

In a recent development, A larger, sculpted alternative to the Viper V4 Pro, the DeathAdder V4 Pro (9/10, WIRED Recommends) is a fantastic mouse that’s a tiny bit heavier, but potentially more comfortable than its smaller cousin. If you prefer the shape and feel of a sculpted mouse, this is a great alternative to Razer’s flagship competitive model that packs comparable performance and is equally-loaded with premium optical internals. The two share the same in-depth customization options, with adjustments for sensitivity curves, lift-off and landing distance, and the ability to adjust the mouse’s rotation for different grip styles.

The Deathadder V4 Pro also introduced Razer’s spherical USB-C dongle with three RGB lights that can be adjusted to display information like polling rate, battery level, connection quality, or DPI. While the colored light system can be a bit abstract, it provides functionality to an accessory that’s going to be on your desk no matter what, and makes it easier to keep track of the settings on this ultra-lightweight mouse. Plus, I find it looks a lot more natural than most dongles available today. Much like other competitive-focused options on this list, the only real issue with this mouse is the lack of Bluetooth connectivity, a weight-savings measure that makes sense for competitive use, but can be a bit annoying for certain consumers and setups that demand more flexibility.

In a recent development, logitech G Pro X3 Superstrike for $200: This is a major advancement in mouse tech, so much so that I’d consider it one of the most significant gaming mouse developments in recent years. This technology replaces the typical mechanical or optical switches under a mouse’s main buttons with analog switches, similar to those on a Hall effect keyboard, that allow for the actuation distance of the button to be customized. Because these linear switches no longer have a “click” sensation, the Superstrike pairs them with artificial haptic feedback. This activates when the button registers an input, and the intensity of the feedback can be customized across X levels.

However, I don’t personally like this mouse. The haptic feedback feels uncanny, since it shakes the entire mouse instead of creating a real “click” sensation, and the added complexity isn’t worth the relatively minor fine-tuning capabilities. However, I can recognize the benefits of the technology, and I can absolutely understand why some people might love this mouse.

Sources indicate that steelseries Rival Pro Wireless for $180: While the specs aren’t groundbreaking compared to other light mice, and the “ultra-polling” technology doesn’t offer a proven benefit over competitors, the Rival Wireless maintains the fantastic shape of previous installments in the Rival 300 line. If you’ve found other sculpted ultralight offerings from Razer and Logitech to be a bit lacking, this could be the option for you.

Recent findings suggest that razer Basilisk V3 Pro for $120: Razer’s previous installment in the Basilisk line is still a really solid option. This mouse is comfortable, convenient, loaded with features, and it looks sleek on any desk. It’s also featured in our Best Ergonomic Mouse guide, but it performs so well that I had to include it here. Razer’s optical sensor is capable of up to 35,000 dpi, and the mouse has polling up to 1,000 Hz (or up to 8,000 Hz with a HyperPolling dongle). As far as comfort and practicality, the Basilisk’s sculpted shape and thumb rest feel more like an office mouse than a gaming mouse, but the curved mouse buttons and smooth overall shape mean a claw grip still isn’t out of the question.

Corsair Sabre V2 Pro Ultralight for $200: When I first reviewed the fresh 36-gram Sabre, I was wowed by its weight but critical of its overly thin shell and flimsy construction. However, I accepted these as being a part of its innate nature as the lightest-possible mouse, and I’m incredibly glad that it exists. It’s a great option if you’re willing to sacrifice everything in the name of “simplifying and adding lightness,” as car designer Colin Chapman put it. But it's probably not the right choice if you want something that feels substantial or meaningful beyond that.

According to recent reports, corsair Sabre V2 Carbon Fiber and Magnesium for $170: While neither of these carry the same groundbreaking lightness of their predecessor (they both hover just below the 60-gram mark), they offer a much more refined design with premium materials and rigidity that’s unmatched by Corsair’s mainstream competitors. While they lag a bit behind in performance, they both feel fantastic to fling around a desk while providing a much more sturdy chassis that gives the impression they can withstand some serious use. Unless you really love the looks or science of carbon fiber, the less-expensive magnesium chassis is definitely the way to go in terms of both sturdiness and on-desk appeal.

It has been revealed that logitech Pro X Superlight 2 Dex for $150: This sculpted mouse predates the Deathadder V4 Pro by over a year and, because of this, the specs lag slightly behind it. However, the shape is just as comfortable, and the internals are still fantastic for anyone except the absolute most-discerning. The best part of this mouse is that, these days, it can easily be found on a significant discount. If you don’t want to shell out the extra cash for Razer’s latest model, or if you prefer Logitech’s software and styling, this is the mouse for you.

According to recent reports, corsair Scimitar Elite Wireless SE for $70: While MMO-focused mice aren’t finding themselves in the spotlight anymore (much like many of the MMOs that required numpads, and even numpads themselves, for that matter), there are still a few new models kicking around. The Scimitar is one of the most modern ones, adding adjustability to the classic numpad-on-the-side formula with a sliding rail to accommodate different grip styles and hand sizes. While this mouse obviously doesn’t compete with other models on this list in terms of technical specs or weight, it’s a really great mouse for the kinds of games that still necessitate having swathes of macros at your fingertips.

Sources indicate that steelseries Aerox 3 for $100: While it doesn’t have nearly the same weight or speed advantages as offerings from Razer and Logitech, the Aerox 3 is still a great mouse in its own special way. Weighing in at only 66 grams and being one of the only waterproof mice on this list (I literally ran it under a sink for a couple minutes to test this), this mouse is great for multi-user gaming computers, accident-prone individuals, and/or the poolside gaming setup of your dreams. Plus, built-in Bluetooth connectivity means you aren’t stuck with a dongle! However, 1000 Hz polling and 18,000 DPI do mean that, if you aren’t looking for something that’s more durable than average, you may be able to get a good bit more performance for a comparable price.

Sources indicate that logitech G203 for $20: Budget gaming mice often forgo a lot of the conveniences and performance you get out of nicer models, but the Logitech G203 never feels like it's lacking. The sensor has a lower maximum sensitivity than you'll get out of a more expensive offering—8,000 dots per inch—so if you need that top-end sensitivity, you'll want to look elsewhere, but it features six buttons, compatibility with Logitech’s G Hub software, and, most importantly, has RGB lighting. Those are all things you'd typically expect to pay more for.

Sources indicate that razer Viper V3 Pro for $100: The previous-gen Viper V3 Pro remains a good choice for competitive gamers, especially since it's selling for much less than the newer model. It remains an uncompromising mouse for lightweight, high-speed gaming performance. Despite being a couple of years old at this point, it still has competitive specs, the same great symmetrical shape, and some of the best-feeling buttons on the market. The battery lasts an incredibly long time (it’s rated for over 95 hours, and I didn’t need to charge it once during my testing). And with the included HyperPolling dongle, the mouse is capable of up to 8,000-Hz polling.

One of the cheapest things you can do to upgrade your PC gaming experience is to invest in a high-quality mousepad. If you’re a mouse-and-keyboard gamer, having the right surface for your trusty little rodent can be super helpful. Not only do you have a nice little area of your desk cordoned off for mouse use, but you also get a surface designed to be as friction-free and slick as possible—so you’ll be as quick as possible.

Harber London Professional Leather Desk Mat.

In a recent development, harber London Professional Leather Desk Mat for $239: Despite more than a year of use, this Harber London leather desk mat still looks exquisite. The pebbled leather is supple and has a nice texture, but your mouse will glide over it effortlessly. It comes in three sizes and three colors.

In a recent development, steelSeries QcK Mouse Pad for $11: SteelSeries’ QcK mousepad is one of my all-time favorites. The medium size is perfect for most desks, even small ones. It’s well-made and doesn’t fray easily—cheaper mousepads often fray at the edges, which ruins the aesthetic a good mousepad can lend to a workstation.

Sources indicate that grovemade Wool Felt Desk Pad for $70: This doesn't seem like your usual gaming accessory, because it's not. It's a wool felt pad from Portland, Oregon, company Grovemade, and it's large enough to fit a keyboard and a mouse with room to spare. It feels soft and plush under your wrists, and all of the gaming mice on this list just glide over its surface; it's like they're sliding on glass. It's a major surprise, honestly. Not to mention, a felt desk pad adds an air of sophistication and style to any desk, without making it seem too uptight. The color looks amazing under RGB lighting in a dark room. It's an easy and affordable way to inject some unique style into your work (and play) space.

What Makes a Good Gaming Mouse?

Here are a few features that really separate a gaming mouse from a regular came-with-my-PC kind of mouse:.

Extra-sensitive optical sensors: Gaming mice should have more sensitive optical sensors that can detect smaller movements more promptly than a standard mouse.

In a recent development, more buttons: At a minimum, a good gaming mouse should have a clickable scroll wheel, a button for adjusting sensitivity, and two buttons where your thumb rests. Those extra thumb buttons can be lifesavers in competitive games.

Sources indicate that better buttons: They should also have higher-quality buttons, and more of them, than a standard office mouse. The left and right buttons should have individual switches inside, tensioned to register rapid clicks and reinforced to withstand more frequent clicks than a normal mouse. Top-of-the-line gaming mice often feature proprietary mechanical switches inside that give them a more tactile feel when you click.

Polling rate: For most games, the typical 1,000-Hz polling rate will be sufficient, but if you play a lot of fast-paced competitive games, where split-second actions can be crucial to victory, than you may get some benefit out of mice with faster polling rates.

Don't buy the DPI hype: Dots per inch (DPI) is a metric that describes a mouse’s overall sensitivity. A higher dpi means it can respond quicker, which is helpful in competitive online games. However, even if your mouse can go all the way up to, say, 20,000 dpi, most people (even in online games) keep their sensitivity around 1,000 to 1,600 dpi. More doesn’t necessarily mean better.

Your Palm Size and Grip Style Matters.

A major aspect when shopping for a gaming mouse is size. Using a mouse that’s too small for your hand can cause strain on your hand and wrist, while a mouse that’s too large can feel unwieldy and be difficult to move precisely. It’s notable to measure your hand and take into account the grip style you strategy to use.

There are three primary mouse grips: Palm grip, claw grip, and fingertip grip. Palm grip is typically considered the most accurate but least agile, and it’s how most people use their mouse day-to-day. Your entire hand sits on the mouse, with your palm resting on the back half and your fingers laid along the mouse buttons. Claw grip is more agile, but will sacrifice some accuracy and stability. For this grip, you rest the bottom of your hand against the mouse while bending your fingers into a claw-like shape, leaving a significant amount of open air between your fingertips and the back of your hand. Fingertip grip has the least contact and allows for the most agility, but also sacrifices even more stability. With this grip, your hand will hover over the mouse, with your fingertips resting on the mouse buttons, and your thumb and pinky finger gripping the mouse from either side.

Recent findings suggest that for a standard mouse used with a palm grip, the best way to determine the correct size is to measure the distance from the tip of your middle finger to the bottom of your palm, and compare those numbers to an online guide. Rocket Jump Ninja has a helpful tool for this, which also provides measurements of the recommended mice for cross-referencing. Alternatively, I’ve found it helpful to hold your hand in an arc as if you’re holding a mouse, and measure the distance from the bottom of your palm to your fingertips to get a measurement you can directly compare to mouse length. This method can also work for claw grip, but since the bottom of your palm will be resting directly on the mouse instead of sitting at the back, I find it better to err on the side of caution and pick a mouse that’s a few millimeters longer than you need.

Recent findings suggest that mouse sizing is dependent on the type of mouse you’re looking for: Whether chasing lightness or portability, there are quite a few short and small mice on the market. Compact or fingertip-grip mice like the Razer Basilisk Mobile or the G-Wolves Fenrir won’t fit the standard recommendations of mouse measurements. Instead, for a mouse like this (or any mouse you strategy to use with a fingertip grip), I find it best to compare the mouse’s width to the distance between your thumb and your pinky finger (or your ring finger, depending on how you hold a mouse) in a comfortable gripping position. A mouse that’s too narrow can cause strain on your hand, while one that’s too wide can be difficult to properly grip and move.

A First Drive With the Fiat Topolino in Newly introduced York City

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1841 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Fiat Topolino isn't exactly built for New York City.
  • Sources indicate that it has a max speed of 25 miles per hour, a 46-mile range, and no airbags.
  • “It's a little bit of an experiment,” says Andrew Waterhouse, head of brand at Fiat USA.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Fiat Topolino isn't exactly built for New York City. Fiat has been selling this tiny electric vehicle in Europe for three years, but it's now arriving in the US for $14,985 as a street-legal micromobility vehicle. Except it's more like a golf cart than a small EV.

Sources indicate that it has a max speed of 25 miles per hour, a 46-mile range, and no airbags. Classified as a “Low Speed Vehicle (LSV),” it can only operate on roads with a posted speed limit of 35 mph or less. (You still need a driver's license, and the Topolino must be registered and have auto insurance.) It also doesn't have a traditional EV charging plug; instead, it uses a 10-foot AC plug that works in any wall outlet—which can be tough if you're in a Brooklyn apartment.

“It's a little bit of an experiment,” says Andrew Waterhouse, head of brand at Fiat USA. “This segment of micromobility—and that's really golf carts—based on the data we have, it's going to grow 28 percent in the next 5 years. People are driving golf carts not to play golf—they're driving them to go to the beach, to go to the clubhouse, to go get coffee, dinner, but they're all just generic. Topolino adds a little bit of that Italian flair and charm, and it's just so unique.”.

That’s hard to refute. There's nothing like the Topolino on the market, EV or otherwise. Its adorable looks have drawn the attention of passersby, who've flicked me a thumbs up as I drove past, or pulled out their phones to sneak a quick pic. The Topolino (which is Italian for “little mouse,” and also what Italians call Mickey Mouse) comes with a lot of compromises, but I've had a blast piloting this thing around the city.

From my conversation with Waterhouse, it was clear that Fiat expects to sell more of these Topolino cars in places like suburban Florida. Gated communities, large residences with private land, homes by the beach—you get the idea. There are also hopes to turn the Topolino into a fleet vehicle for campuses and the like. But I wanted to see what it would be like in the bustling streets of Latest York City. After all, I already drive the Fiat 500 as my personal vehicle.

The Fiat Topolino, left, next to the already small Fiat 500, right.

The first thing that surprised me—other than the minuscule size, which you won't stop thinking about—is how plasticky the thing is. I leaned on it for a second and felt the plastic exterior sink in a little, which immediately made me realize the Topolino won't handle a crash very well; no crumple zones, no airbags—just seatbelts. So yes, don't take this thing on the highway.

It's built for two people and not much else. The passenger can stow a suitcase in front of them, and there's a rack on the back of the car to store another. But besides mesh pouches in the door frames and an elongated glove compartment on top of the dashboard that runs the width of the car, that's about it for storage.

Sources indicate that I should also mention the Topolino comes in a few variants: The standard model I tried has full doors and a fixed glass roof, but there's an Open Air model with a roll-back soft-top roof, and the Dolce Vita model has rope doors (aka no doors) and the soft-top roof. You can buy the car in mint, orange, or brownish-gray.

Thankfully, despite my 6'4" frame, I fit quite comfortably in the Topolino. I do have to swing my leg under the steering wheel as I get in, and the seats are a little firm, but the inside feels quite roomy. Only the driver's seat can move forward or back—the passenger seat stays put, and you cannot adjust the steering wheel height.

In a recent development, the asymmetrical, reverse-hinged doors are very unique. The driver's side opens outward from the front, and the passenger door opens the opposite way. There's also a button on each side to open the door, and weirdly, to get out, you pull a fabric strap. Now, the driver-side strap is to the left of the steering wheel, which makes sense, but the passenger-side strap is in an awkward spot behind the seat, near the seatbelt strap. A few of my passengers found that annoying. Also annoying is that you need to use the key to unlock both doors individually—no auto-unlock button plus no key fob. (The car starts with a second key.).

Recent findings suggest that the horizontally split, manually hinged windows flip up, but on rougher roads, they tend to flip back down. You can adjust the small, circular side mirrors and the rear-view mirror, which also doubles as a backup camera display. I have found the backup camera mostly useless, especially at night, when it's just really hard to see what’s going on.

Good thing visibility in the Topolino is excellent, so it's really easy to swing your head around. Unsurprisingly, you can park this thing anywhere. I've parallel parked the Topolino in several tight spots that no other car can fit in, and the lack of parking sensors or the lackluster backup camera didn't bother me. In a city as crowded as New York, that's incredibly valuable.

Industry observers note that you should know there's no air-conditioning or heating. There's a windshield fan to defog the windows, which, along with the single wiper and wiper fluid, was useful on cold, rainy days. But in the winter months, you'll have to bundle up, or in the summer, affix a battery-powered (or USB-C) fan to the dashboard. On the dash, you have a simple instrument cluster that shows speed and remaining range, and a built-in phone mount to the right.

You can store luggage on the rack—there's no trunk.

Industry observers note that turn the key to start the car, disengage the parking brake, and tap D or R to start driving. There's no power steering, so turning the wheel requires a little more force than you're used to, and the turn signals don't automatically disengage after you turn. Still, the car feels very responsive. The 8-horsepower electric motor feels fairly quick when you put the pedal to the metal, though you promptly hit the Topolino’s top speed. Good thing the default speed limit in Newly introduced York City is 25 mph.

Recent findings suggest that but as you start driving, you'll experience arguably the worst thing about the Fiat Topolino: the sound. Because of federal regulations around electric LSVs, the Topolino has a pedestrian alert sound—the kind of angelic hum you might have heard when an electric car is reversing or rolling up to a stop sign. Except the sound is constant, and it gets louder the faster you go. I'm not sure why it's so loud in the car. It feels like it's alerting me more than pedestrians around me.

Recent findings suggest that the sound only disappears if you go past 22 mph, which isn't often, since streets in most cities have a stop sign or traffic light after every block. The first time my wife and I rode in the car, we could barely hear each other talk over the hum. You get used to it over time, but it's very annoying. You can try playing music over it, but the car has no speaker system. Instead, Fiat sells a pair of Monster Bluetooth speakers that you can magnetically stick to the top frame of the car. That works OK, but I didn't like having to keep them charged, so when they died, I played music from my phone. It was sad.

You can fit the Topolino anywhere!

The ride is a little stiff. I drove over one of the worst roads in Brooklyn (Broadway), and you could feel every single bump. When I drove with my brother, they often just exclaimed “Jesus!” every few minutes. Cobblestone was equally pretty bad. But it's doable, and on well-maintained roads, the Topolino was a smooth ride.

Recent findings suggest that new Yorkers rejoice! You legally cannot drive this car into New Jersey. (As if you needed a reason.) All of the bridges and tunnels to the Garden State have speed limits higher than 35 mph. However, I could take the East River bridges to go from Brooklyn to Manhattan, and I did exactly that. Driving over the Manhattan Bridge was a little terrifying when I was holding up a few cars in my lane and everyone decided to race around me. But I got a few thumbs-ups along the way, which helped. Everyone finds this car cute, which goes a long way toward how people treat you on the road.

As for range, it's not great. I wish it were closer to 80 miles instead of 46 miles, especially at this price. It's perfect for quick hour-long round trips around the city; anything longer will give you range anxiety. That trip over the bridge? I went from Bed-Stuy, Brooklyn, to Lower Manhattan and back (around 12 miles). The indicated remaining range went from 46 miles to 30 by the time I got home.

In a recent development, recharging takes around five hours from zero to full, and the charging cord is built into the car near the passenger-side door. Annoyingly, the 10-foot cable isn't retractable, so you awkwardly have to stuff it back into the door frame when you're done. But the bigger issue is the length. And the standard AC plug. EV charging stations don't typically have AC outlets like the ones in your home. And 10 feet is far too short to reach any apartment or residence in New York City.

Charging the Fiat Topolino requires a standard wall outlet—and, in Brooklyn, probably a long extension cord.

I bought a 50-foot extension cord and ran the cable from my outdoor parking spot to my backyard outlet. It worked perfectly well, but I'm also an outlier, with access to a parking spot and a backyard. Most people don't have those luxuries, so you'll need your own solution.

Initially, after my first ride with the Topolino, I was apprehensive. It felt like I was sitting in a plastic box on wheels, with a blaring sound that wouldn't stop, and every significant bump sending a shock into my body. After a week, I was driving the thing everywhere, hand dangling out the half-window, fist-bumping other drivers in bumper-to-bumper traffic, and parking in the tiniest available spots around Brooklyn. Now, a week without the little mouse, I miss it dearly.

It's far from the perfect city car. There are small things I would change to improve the overall rideability. And like the Fiat 500e, it's way too expensive. But as someone who likes their car to stand out, I find so much of what's available in the US market uninspiring. The Topolino breaks the mold. We need more small cars like it.

Breaking: Own Your Intelligence: A How-To Guide

📅 19 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1462 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sequoiacap

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the race for the AI application layer is not only about UI, workflows, or GTM...
  • According to recent reports, the race for the AI application layer is not only about UI, workflows, or GTM...
  • The calls for owning your intelligence are escalatingâ¦.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the race for the AI application layer is not only about UI, workflows, or GTM... it is a fight for the intelligence layer itself.

According to recent reports, the race for the AI application layer is not only about UI, workflows, or GTM... it is a fight for the intelligence layer itself.

The calls for owning your intelligence are escalatingâ¦.

Recently, Alex Karp encouraged enterprises to âown the means of production.â Not long after, Satya Nadella declared that buying intelligence from a frontier lab is like paying twice: once with money, and once with the proprietary knowledge you reveal to make that intelligence useful.

The question everyone is asking: who should own the intelligence at the core of your business?

According to recent reports, to be clear, owning your intelligence is not a mandate nor a recommendation to get off the labs. For many workloads, frontier APIs and agents are still the right answer. But across our portfolio, we are seeing more companies building their own AI capabilities for parts of their products, vertically integrating toward owning and shaping their weights.

In a recent development, A few weeks ago, Sequoia brought together a group of AI founders and builders for an event on owning your AI stack. We had Harvey give us the customer-back view. Then Mercor, Langchain, Trajectory, and Fireworks walked us through the technical building blocks in the post-training stack.

Across the talks, a clear playbook emerged.

In a recent development, first, the open-weight frontier has moved faster than anticipated. Kimi K3 and GLM 5.2 are extremely good! Training on open models used to be a treadmillâ¦ you mightâve spent months fine-tuning, and the next frontier release would erase your gains. Now, you can start from a baseline close to the frontier.

In a recent development, second, the independent post-training stack has matured. Thanks to companies like Mercor and Fireworks, every company can access the technology stack of a frontier research lab, from training to inference to human or synthetic data. With strong evals, harness engineering, post-training, and online learning, open models can now beat frontier models in specific domains.

A year ago, you chose open weights when performance was something you could sacrifice. Now, it is becoming an existential and strategic question. The newest battleground is for the intelligence layer. Not your weights, not your product.

Thereâs no one-size-fits-all approach. In addition to performance, there may be slices of your product where renting intelligence becomes a constraint because ofâ¦.

Recent findings suggest that 1. Cost. The more successful your AI product, the higher your AI COGS. If inference costs scale directly with usage, owning the model is the best way to protect your margins.

2. Speed. If youâre operating in a domain like coding (tab autocomplete) or cybersecurity, a small distilled custom model might beat a large general one, because speed is so important.

3. Proprietary data. If your feedback, evals, customer interactions, or domain data are what make the system better, you might prefer that data stays within your walls.

4. Controlling your destiny. The app layer and the intelligence layer are starting to merge. The labs are moving up into product, and app companies are moving down into the training loops that define how the product thinks. Owning the product increasingly might mean controlling more of the learning loop and the intelligence itself (h/t Harvey Research, RampLabs, Glean, Factory, and more).

Assuming you've decided on your strategy for what to own vs. rent, the question becomes: how do you go from zero to one?

According to recent reports, build your team. Don't shoehorn this into a platform team. Owning your intelligence needs people playing offense: building evals, shaping data, experimenting with open models, tuning harnesses, and pushing performance in a domain. Small, de novo teams go very far here, partnering with half a dozen ecosystem partners. Harvey, for example, has done a surprising amount of research with a team of just seven people!

Make the work legible. Every buyer right now is choosing their AI champion. Increasingly, the tiebreaker is published research, benchmarks, or technical posts. If you choose to do wonderful research in-house, share it with the ecosystem.

Execute the technical steps. Weâve laid out a high level framework below.

Harveyâs Gabe Pereyra said it well: "If you don't have a good benchmark, you can't train models.â.

In a recent development, an eval is a set of tasks that measures whether your system can do the work well. Every task contains a prompt, context the model can use, and a grader. Most evals start as a founder squinting at outputs and vibe-checking whether they feel right. The goal is to turn that judgement into something repeatable.

Industry observers note that harvey built its Legal Agent Benchmark by turning real legal work into discrete tasks a model could be tested on. The first iteration includes more than 1,200 agent tasks across 24 legal practice areas, and is evaluated by over 75,000 expert-written rubric criteria.

Itâs crucial to have an eval before making the decision to own your intelligence. Once every forward pass has an eval, deciding which model to use can be a measured decision instead of a guess.

2/ Harness and context engineering.

In a recent development, an agent has three parts: the model, the context, and the harness. The harness governs the product logic around the model: routing, retrieval, tools, memory, fallbacks, and traces. Harrison Chaseâs simple framing was that "the main job of the harness is to bring context to the model at the right point in time." The more out of distribution the task is for the model, the worse the off-the-shelf harness will be.

Industry observers note that A good harness lets you route tasks to the best model for your specific job, reuse the same evals across models, and decide what context and tools an agent gets. It also makes the agent inspectable. You can trace what context went in, which tools were called, and where it got stuck.

Post-training covers several techniques. The right one depends on what youâre trying to improve.

Sources indicate that lin Qiao laid it out: if the model is missing facts, you don't need to post-train - just use context or RAG. If the output format or behavior is wrong, use supervised fine-tuning. If the glitch is product taste, use preference tuning. If the model needs to improve at a specialized task, use RL. If the model is too slow or expensive, distill it.

The goal is to pick the lightest method that moves your eval. Then serve the model through the same harness and measure quality, latency, and cost as it runs.

Once the system has its pieces â evals, harness, and model â the final step is improving that system in production.

Arjun Karanam made a good point: models keep getting smarter, but every session feels like it's their first day on the job. You can put Terence Tao in an accounting firm, but chances are (at least on day 1) he wonât be the best accountant there. What's missing is experience, not intelligence. Agents create that experience as they run.

A trajectory is the path through the task: the context the model saw, the tools and sub-agents it called, the answer it produced, and what the user edited, undid, or retried. Capturing those trajectories in a tool like LangChain's LangSmith is necessary to build a continuous production loop. A failed task becomes an eval. Missing information goes into context or memory. A bad tool response becomes a harness fix.

Buyer beware: owning your intelligence opens Pandoraâs box.

The closed-model stack is simple. You call a frontier model, use an out-of-the-box harness (e.g., Claude Code or Codex), add prompts and context, and ship. That gives you a high floor, but also a lower ceiling.

Owning your stack means taking on more of the system yourself. The production stack becomes your open-source model, custom harness, tools, and context. The development stack becomes your proprietary evals, domain data, and online learning loop.

Industry observers note that it is certainly more work! It potentially gives you a lower floor â but it also raises the ceiling.

The labs will keep building the giant brains. We should all use them.

It has been revealed that but, in parallel, the best product companies are growing their own little geniuses: fast, opinionated, domain-obsessed, and tuned to the work they see. In a world where more companies take ownership of their own intelligence, the ecosystem flourishes and individuality triumphs.

Thatâs the promise of a world where companies own their intelligence. And weâre delighted to see the progress from the little guys, the startups that want to bring that world into existence.

#38066. 8 Best Keyboards (2026): My Honest Picks After Testing Dozens

📅 18 May 2019 • ⏱️ 28m • 📚 Deep Dive (5613 w)
